title: Hardwired and microprogrammed control
kicker: ENCT 303 · Computer Organization and Architecture · Chapter 3
subtitle: The control unit turns an opcode into the exact sequence of signals that move data through the machine.

sections.title: Micro-operations
sections.body: An instruction is carried out as a sequence of micro-operations, each a register-transfer that fits in one clock. Fetch, for example, is: MAR ← PC; MDR ← Memory[MAR]; IR ← MDR; PC ← PC + 1. A control word is the set of signals (which register loads, which bus is driven, what the ALU does) asserted in one step.

choices.text: The bundle of control signals asserted during one micro-operation step.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each bit enables a register load, selects a bus source or picks an ALU function.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The opcode chooses which sequence of control words to issue.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Data travels on the data path; control words steer it.

figures.caption: Figure 3.1.1 — instruction fetch
figures.note: Four micro-operations make up instruction fetch.

sections.title: Hardwired control
sections.body: A hardwired control unit generates signals with combinational logic: a step counter decoded to timing signals T1, T2…, an opcode decoder, and gates that AND them together (e.g. “load IR = T3”). It is very fast, but changing the instruction set means redesigning the logic — the usual choice for RISC.

choices.text: Speed — signals come straight out of gates with no memory lookup.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Complex instruction sets need a lot of logic.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The price is that it is hard to modify.

sections.title: Microprogrammed control
sections.body: In a microprogrammed unit the control words are stored in a fast control memory. Each instruction’s opcode selects the start of a microroutine; a micro-program counter steps through it, reading one microinstruction per clock and sending its bits to the data path. A microinstruction also says what comes next: fall through, jump, or branch on a condition flag. Changing or extending the instruction set is just rewriting the microcode (Wilkes’ original idea), which is why CISC machines use it.

worked.why: A machine has 64 micro-routines of at most 16 microinstructions each and 40 control signals.
Control memory holds 64 × 16 = 1024 words. Each word carries the 40 signals plus a next-address field of ⌈log₂1024⌉ = 10 bits.

questions.prompt: Why do CISC designers like microprogramming?

choices.text: New or complex instructions are added by writing microcode, not redesigning logic.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Flexibility is bought with an extra memory lookup per step.

figures.caption: Figure 3.3.1 — microprogrammed control unit

sections.title: Horizontal and vertical microcode
sections.body: Horizontal microinstructions give every control signal its own bit: wide, fast, highly parallel. Vertical ones encode the signals in fields (like opcodes) and need decoders: narrow but slower. Real designs mix them.

choices.text: Wide, with one bit per control signal.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: That allows many micro-operations in the same clock.

sections.title: Sequencing the microprogram
sections.body: After each microinstruction the next address comes from: the incremented µPC (most steps), a jump field, a conditional branch on a flag, a mapping from the opcode (at the start), or a stack for microsubroutines. Address generation is the control unit’s own program counter logic.

questions.prompt: Which source normally supplies the next microaddress?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Most microinstructions simply fall through to the next word.

figures.caption: Figure 3.5.1 — microinstruction sequencing
figures.script:
diagram("direction: down
(Fetch microroutine) as f
[Map opcode to start] as m
<Condition met?> as c
[µPC ← branch target] as b
[µPC ← µPC + 1] as n
(Execute next microinstruction) as e
f -> m
m -> c
c -> b : yes
c -> n : no
b -> e
n -> e");

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Instructions = sequences of micro-operations; a control word drives one step.
  • Hardwired: fast, rigid. Microprogrammed: flexible, a bit slower.
  • Horizontal = wide and parallel; vertical = narrow and encoded.
